extracted.intended_audience: scientists and educated general readers interested in psychometrics, anthropometry, heredity, and eugenics (late 19th-century)
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of the evaluative criteria, methods, and methodological cautions found in Francis Galton's Inquiries into Human Faculty and Its Development — covering anthropometry, psychometric experiments, composite portraiture, statistical methods, heredity, and policies on selection/eugenics. Useful for assessing historical scientific methods and standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction — purpose and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The book is intended to be suggestive rather than encyclopedic; it brings together memoirs on hereditary faculties, defines cardinal points, and aims to consider whether it might be our duty to aid evolution by supplanting inefficient human stock with better strains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorial intent: proceed like a surveyor of a new country; fix positions of cardinal points, avoid exhaustive detail in places (esp. anthropometry) and present methods and cautions for those who may pursue them further.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety of human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Human instincts and faculties differ widely; many diverse varieties may each be good of their kind, and it would be harmful to force assimilation to a single common type, though some hereditary elements are of little value or harmful and admit of improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious of ethnocentric bias; do not take one culture's instincts as universal standard; recognise both valuable variety and traits that may merit selective improvement; specify a few hereditary characteristics and methods of appraising them rather than exhaustive lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Features (physiognomy) — limits of measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Facial expression is the sum of a multitude of very small traits; individual differences are numerous and mostly too minute for measurement. Selecting 'typical' individuals by judgement is fallacious and tends to produce caricatures rather than true types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid selecting representatives by subjective judgement; a 'typical' face is elusive; measurement should account for many small traits; anecdotal or fashion-influenced assessments can mislead about prevailing types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composite portraiture — principle and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Composite portraiture brings into evidence traits in which there is agreement and reduces individual peculiarities by superimposing many portraits to obtain an 'ideal average' face; the method reveals the prevalent type better than selecting portraits judged typical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use composites to counter selection bias; ensure careful photographic technique to prevent dominance of any single component; compare composites with components to validate results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composite portraiture — method (earlier method steps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Steps: (1) collect portraits photographed in same aspect and lighting; (2) reduce portraits to same size guided by reference distances (e.g., between pupils and lips); (3) superimpose portraits so features align; (4) fasten into a book and expose each page in succession to the camera without moving it; (5) allow only a fraction of exposure to each portrait so combined image forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control scale by anatomical reference points; keep camera fixed; use brief exposures per component; later methods are more complex and detailed in Appendix. Watch for careless photography causing one face to dominate; remaking composites without a component can test robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composite portraiture — interpretation and cautions
rubrics_metrics.description: Composite pictures emphasize common traits and leave a 'ghost' of individuality; with care they do not allow a single portrait to dominate; observers often misattribute dominance to a particular component, and removing that component may not change the composite materially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspect composites and components together; test robustness by removing suspected dominant components; larger composites show more individual traces but still reflect central tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bodily qualities (anthropometry)
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of anthropometric data: statistical anomalies in stature dependent on age, town vs. rural populations, athletic feats historically and recently, increase of stature in middle classes, prevalence of weakly persons; physical faculties are closely tied to moral/intellectual faculties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect anthropometric measurements systematically (see 'Anthropometric Registers'); beware of deceptive appearances of weakness; interpret bodily data in social and historical context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Energy as an evaluative attribute
rubrics_metrics.description: Energy is an attribute of 'high races'; stimuli to activity and the preservation of weakly persons (for pity or sport) affect societal fitness; energy is considered useful and a desirable trait.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing 'race' or families, consider energy/activity levels; recognise social practices that preserve weakly individuals may influence future stock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity (sensation and pain) — measurement scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Range and grades of sensation vary; tests must recognise that they measure state of faculties at time of trial; there are cautions about constructing tests and multiplicity of perceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design sensory tests with attention to temporal state-dependence; account for individual differences (idiots, the blind, sailors) and vocabulary limitations in expressing gradations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence of test weights (psychophysical method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a geometric series of weights and a defined method of presentation; the same principle applies to other senses. Tests only measure faculties at time of trial; construct test weights with caution; multiple perceptions complicate measurement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply geometric progression for discriminability tests; include cautions about momentary state, fatigue, and cross-modality issues; see Appendix C for apparatus and detailed protocol.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whistles for audibility of shrill notes (test apparatus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construction and use of whistles to test the upper limits of audibility in individuals; hearing of high notes declines with age; trials on animals show varying sensitivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standardise whistle construction and testing conditions; account for age-related decline; compare across species where informative; see Appendix D for design and procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anthropometric registers (data collection standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is want of anthropometric laboratories and family records; opportunities exist in schools and naval records; family registers and ancestral life-histories are valuable for eugenics and medical use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish systematic, institutional anthropometric recording (e.g., school, Admiralty) and preserve family life-histories; autotypes and registers facilitate longitudinal study and eugenic assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unconsciousness of peculiarities (detection and heredity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Traits such as colour-blindness and peculiarities of mental imagery are often unsuspected by their possessors; some peculiarities are hereditary (e.g., colour blindness in Quakers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use targeted inquiries and tests to uncover unsuspected traits; consider family histories to trace heredity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical methods — objects and curve-fitting
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistical science aims at constancy and continuity of results; groups and sub-groups often show ogival (sigmoid) curves; methods for comparing ogival groups and centesimal grading are described; a pricker can be used to make statistical records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply ogival curve-fitting for distributional analysis; use first and second methods of comparison (described in text); employ centesimal grading for relative scaling; simple tools like a pricker can record data efficiently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character — observation and variability
rubrics_metrics.description: Character traits (e.g., caprice, coyness) vary by sex and education; causes include schooling and social environment; aversions and likings are not universal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess character through systematic observation (school studies noted); avoid overgeneralisation from cultural anecdotes; investigate variation across contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminals and the insane — descriptive standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Some peculiarities of criminal character are normal, not morbid; inheritance of criminal traits (e.g., Jukes) is discussed; epileptics show nervous instability; insanity presents moody segregation and altered individuality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between morally deviant but normal variants and genuine pathology; collect family and life-histories to trace heredity; examine environmental and social factors (e.g., celibacy, solitude) that correlate with insanity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gregarious and slavish instincts — social behavioural criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Many humans shrink from responsibility; study of herding animals yields principles about herd size, leader production, and conditions of safety; similar principles applied to tribes and political behaviour produce servility or leadership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating social systems, consider instinctive tendencies for gregariousness and servility; assess how social structure shapes leaders and followers and the statistical constancy of corporate actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual differences — heredity and assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to Hereditary Genius and the role of hereditary factors in intellectual merit; families and strains are compared for success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use genealogical and achievement records to appraise intellectual differences; consider both heredity and nurture influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental imagery — survey and analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigations via circular of questions reveal wide variation in visualising faculty; answers analysed (octile, median) and examples extracted; imagery is hereditary, varies by sex and nationality, can be educated, and typically lacks flexibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use structured questionnaires and statistical analysis to classify imagery strength; corroborate with different populations; recognise potential exaggeration in self-report; consult Appendix E for the circular of questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number-forms — identification and description
rubrics_metrics.description: Number-forms (personal spatial arrangements of numbers) show great variety, are sometimes hereditary, can be illustrated and classified, and have implications for cognitive mapping (colours assigned to numerals, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect self-reports and illustrative drawings; classify forms and note familial patterns; consider cross-cultural frequency (Talmud reference) and developmental origins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colour associations — cross-modal associations
rubrics_metrics.description: Associations of colours with numerals, words, and letters vary widely between individuals; some schemes are unintelligible to others; mental music and synesthetic links are reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document associations with plates and examples (Plate IV); compare reports across respondents and corroborate with external testimony (Dr. J. Key).

rubrics_metrics.name: Visionaries — distinction from vivid visualisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Sane persons often see visions; visions differ from visualisations and may be based on patched or blended recollections; causes include fasting, spiritual discipline, and hereditary tendencies; hallucinations of great men noted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate visions/hallucinations from ordinary vivid imagery; gather histories of onset (e.g., fasting, solitude); consider hereditary prevalence and historical periods of higher incidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nurture and nature — interaction and separation difficulty
rubrics_metrics.description: Effects of nurture and nature are difficult to separate; the same character manifests many phases and changes can follow cultural fashions; childhood impressions are deep and formative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use twin studies, family histories, and historical comparisons to disentangle effects; avoid simplistic attribution to either factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Associations — origin and classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Associations derive from experience, especially childhood; abstract and cumulative ideas (e.g., composite portraits) have resemblance in details and can be systematically studied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect associative data (see psychometric methods); classify associations (abstract, concrete, cumulative) and relate them to developmental history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychometric experiments — method and classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Difficult to watch the mind in operation; methods developed to overcome this include tentative experiments and subsequent refined methods; number of recurrent associations, memory, ages at formation, and classification of association types are reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use controlled experimental procedures, repeated trials, and classification schemes; record frequencies and ages; be aware of subject fatigue/irksomeness and design tolerable regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antechamber of consciousness — analysis of thinking process
rubrics_metrics.description: Thinking involves automatic mental work preceding consciousness; fluency of words and imagery, processes of literary composition, and phenomena of inspiration and morbid ideas are analysed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying mental processes, attend to subconscious automatic operations and their role in creative production; differentiate normal fluency from pathological enthusiasm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early sentiments — formation and transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: Early sentiments arise from accidents of education, religion, and country; religion instils prejudices and fear of death; aversions are easily taught and affect entire classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider early environmental shaping when assessing adult dispositions; compare across religious and cultural practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: History of twins — comparative method for nature vs nurture
rubrics_metrics.description: Twin histories provide means to compare effects of nurture and nature; many cases show close resemblance, interchangeability, parallel lives, and occasional great dissimilarity (sometimes due to illness). Education is almost powerless to erase natural differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use twin data systematically to assess heritability; document similarities and divergences, note illness/developmental interruptions, and beware of slight exaggeration in anecdotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestication of animals — criteria for domestication
rubrics_metrics.description: Domestication possible when species have natural faculties: great hardiness, fondness for man, desire of comfort, usefulness, fertility, ease of tending. Habitual selection of tamest for breeding is typical; exceptions and worldwide examples given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When inferring domestication processes, evaluate species by listed criteria; examine ethnographic instances and consider selection practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: The observed order of events — teleology and human agency
rubrics_metrics.description: There is steady improvement of successive generations; man can expedite evolution and may have a duty to do so; importance of life-histories is emphasised for guiding interventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame policy and scientific interventions with awareness of long-term evolutionary processes; collect life-histories to inform action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and race — concepts and trade-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: Difference exists between best specimens of poor races and mediocre of high races; highly-bred animals can be delicate and less fertile; rigorous selection causes misery; replacing poor races by better ones may be preferable in some views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing selection policies, weigh fitness trade-offs (vigour vs fertility), ethical costs of rigorous selection, and practical alternatives (replacement, admixture).

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of man upon race — migrations, conquest, and prejudice
rubrics_metrics.description: Man influences race via conquest and migration; sentiment against extinguishing races is partly unreasonable; historical examples (Moors, Gypsies, Damara land) show variety and changeability of races.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy assessments should consider historical mixing, diffusion, and social attitudes; use demographic and historical evidence to evaluate claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Population — critique of Malthus and over-population
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of over-population and Malthus: danger of applying prudential checks, originality of Malthus, and that his 'misery check' is sometimes too severe; causes of decaying races considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply population theory with caution; examine local conditions before advocating prudential checks; consider demographic and racial health trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early and late marriages — demographic effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate of relative effects of early vs late marriages on a population over a few generations with example computations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use demographic modelling to assess generational impact of marriage timing; incorporate fertility and survival assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marks for family merit — selection indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposal to suggest outlines for marking family merit: signs of superior race, weight given to family antecedents when candidates are personally equal, families that have thriven, healthy and long-lived families may be markers of merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect family antecedents and confer marks based on family merit; recognise current paucity of knowledge about family backgrounds and call for further inquiry; be cautious about fairness and measurement validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endowments — social incentives for suitable marriages
rubrics_metrics.description: Endowments and adopted marriage portions have been used to influence marriage choices; college statutes requiring celibacy had reverse effects; reform of statutes changed patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider institutional incentives (endowments, statutes) as levers for influencing reproductive choices; anticipate unintended consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusion — synthesis and recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Epitome of data: man should assist evolution, his current ability to do so will increase, and life-histories are important; brief summary of above points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasise data collection (life-histories), measured intervention, and continued study to inform eugenic policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appendix A — composite portraiture memoirs
rubrics_metrics.description: Contains three memoir extracts giving successive stages of the composite portraiture method, including technical details and examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult Appendix A for full procedural detail, illustrations, and experimental controls when implementing composite methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appendix B — relative supplies from town and country families
rubrics_metrics.description: Memoir on differences in reproductive supplies from town vs country families and implications for future generations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use statistical and demographic records to assess differential reproduction by locale; apply to projections of generational change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appendix C — apparatus for testing weight discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed memoir describing an apparatus and method for testing the delicacy with which weights can be discriminated by handling them (geometric series, procedure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Appendix C for construction details, trial protocol, and cautions about temporal state-dependence of measurements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appendix D — whistles for testing auditory upper limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Memoir describing whistles designed to test upper limits of audible sound in different individuals with construction and trial notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Appendix D designs for standardised auditory testing; record age and species variations; control test environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appendix E — questions on visualising and allied faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: Circular of questions distributed in 1880 to probe visualising ability and related faculties; forms the empirical basis of many analyses in the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use structured questionnaires (Appendix E) for comparative studies of mental imagery; apply statistical aggregation (octile, median) to responses and corroborate with multiple respondent pools.
